articles.title: Older women are as varied and individual as we have ever been | Letters
articles.summary: Thank you, Jo Brand, for not offering us a formula for growing older, writes Dr Denise Taylor. Plus a letter from Louise Mothersole. I found Jo Brand’s reflections on approaching 70 wonderfully refreshing ( ‘It’s far too late for me to go to the gym every 10 minutes’: Jo Brand on ageing, raging…
body: We hear so much about ageing well, ageing positively and ageing successfully. We are encouraged to exercise more, eat better, remain productive, find our purpose and keep reinventing ourselves. Much of this advice is well intentioned, but collectively it can make growing older seem like another job we are expected to perform.

As a 69-year-old psychologist who researches and writes about later life, I question this narrative. Of course, looking after our health matters. But ageing isn’t a competition, and we shouldn’t have to demonstrate that we’re making the most of every remaining year.

I was particularly struck by Brand’s comments about older women being treated as though they are all alike. We are as varied, contradictory and individual as we have ever been. Some of us want adventure; others want a quieter life. Some are still working, others are delighted to have left employment behind. And our feelings about ageing can change from one day to the next.

Perhaps what makes Brand’s interview so appealing is that she doesn’t offer us a formula for growing older. She simply describes her experience, with humour, honesty and a willingness to acknowledge what is difficult.
points: Thank you, Jo Brand, for not offering us a formula for growing older, writes Dr Denise Taylor.

articles.title: Is this the most rubbish Christmas present ever? | Polly Hudson
articles.summary: I thought I knew all about disappointment, having received one of the very worst presents as a child. Then I heard about ‘data gifting’ One Christmas when I was a child, my parents wrapped the presents in shiny paper.
body: The jubilation I felt at pulling off such a stealth move – being basically a master criminal in the manner of those movie jewel thieves who dodge laser tripwires – was almost immediately negated by the sinking realisation I’d ruined my own Christmas. I’d been too impatient to bear the wait, but now, with weeks still to go, all anticipation and excitement had been extinguished. Not least because my main present was – how to put this delicately? – crap.

I always struggled to get up for school, so Santa had stitched me up with an alarm clock. A fun, razzy alarm clock, but an alarm clock all the same. To clarify: no kid wants an alarm clock. It was the very definition of bleak times.

Until this week, I believed this was the most depressing Christmas present in the history of the nativity. But then I heard an advert for a mobile phone provider, which offered the suggestion of “data gifting”. This is where, brimming with festive spirit, you transfer your unused or spare data to somebody else’s device or plan, ho ho ho. A virtual, imaginary present so entirely practical the recipient probably won’t even realise when they use it.

articles.title: What are you yearning for? We took to the streets to find out
articles.summary: Longing for someone – or something – can be even more thrilling than getting what you want. That knowledge has inspired endless movies, but what do real people yearn for? We asked the question in Glasgow.
body: I n a world of instant gratification, is it any surprise that many of us have fallen back in love with the idea of “yearning”? Running counter to much of today’s on-demand culture, yearning melds desire and distance, nostalgia and uncertainty; longing for something, or someone, can sometimes appeal in a way that getting exactly what you want cannot.

The resurgence of yearning – especially in the romantic sense – has been one of the biggest entertainment themes of the last couple of years: from The Summer I Turned Pretty and Heated Rivalry to the latest big-screen adaptation of Sense and Sensibility, the allure of unmet desire and slow-burn love has topped hasty happy-ever-afters. TikTok remains awash with recommendations for those who want to #feeltheyearn.

But yearning encompasses more than just romantic infatuation. You might be pining for a particular place or longing for a different time in life. With this in mind, we took to the streets to ask: what are you yearning for right now?
points: Longing for someone – or something – can be even more thrilling than getting what you want.
That knowledge has inspired endless movies, but what do real people yearn for?

articles.title: Tired all the time? What to know about B12 and if it actually boosts energy levels
articles.summary: Med spas are raving about vitamin B12 shots as a pick-me-up. But do they actually make you feel more energized? If you spend time on social media, you may have seen med spa owners and employees describing vitamin B12 shots as a pick-me-up.
body: B12 is essential to your health, and people who don’t get enough of it can feel exhausted or worse. But most people already have plenty of B12, and for them, extra doses aren’t likely to help.
Here’s what you need to know about what B12 does, who runs low on it and when to get tested.

Vitamin B12 is found naturally in animal foods like meat, fish, eggs and dairy, and it’s added to some breakfast cereals and nutritional yeasts. It helps your body make red blood cells and DNA, and it keeps your nerves working properly. It also plays a role in turning food into energy, which is where its reputation as an energy booster comes from.

When people don’t have enough B12, they can develop anemia, memory problems, depression and fatigue, says Andrea Dean, a hematologist at Loyola University medical center in Chicago. If their levels are seriously low, they can also develop numbness and tingling in their hands and feet.
points: Med spas are raving about vitamin B12 shots as a pick-me-up.
But do they actually make you feel more energized?

articles.title: A Visit With Six Women Farmers Across the Americas
articles.summary: Between January and August 2026, photographer Lys Arango spent two weeks living with each of six women farmers. Her images follow the rhythm of their days and show what these women have built: cooperatives, savings groups, a coffee brand of their own, knowledge passed on to their daughters and…
body: Women make up nearly half of the agricultural workforce in developing countries, yet they account for fewer than one in five of the world’s agricultural landholders. As rising food prices, climate volatility, and food security concerns put farming back at the center of public debate, the United Nations designated 2026 as the International Year of the Woman Farmer, bringing renewed attention to a workforce that remains central to food systems while often excluded from land ownership, financing, and decision-making.

María Espinoza, 54, lives in the highlands of San Cristóbal Island, in the Galápagos. She is up at 5 a.m. to feed her animals before heading into the fields, where she grows fruit and vegetables on a plot she slowly reclaimed from invasive blackberry. She lives alone but the farm sets the rhythm of her day, keeps her company, and puts food on the table.

Fresh water on the island is scarce and depends on El Junco lagoon, while pests and food shipped in from the mainland make farming hard. María uses no chemicals, makes her own organic fertilizers, and, since 2023, has trained in protecting soil and crops without pesticides.

articles.title: The Deeper Meaning Behind Kate Middleton’s Remembrance Day Earrings
articles.summary: Over two days of remembrance, the Princess of Wales paid tribute to Queen Elizabeth II and Princess Diana through two particularly meaningful pieces of jewelry.
body: Kate Middleton’s jewelry choices often carry a significance beyond their sparkle. Across this year’s Remembrance commemorations, the Princess of Wales paid subtle tributes to two of the most significant women in the royal family’s history: Queen Elizabeth II and Princess Diana. And the personal stories behind her chosen earrings offered a poignant reminder of how royal jewels are passed between generations.

On Sunday morning, Kate joined senior members of the royal family for the National Service of Remembrance at London’s Cenotaph, where King Charles III and Prince William laid wreaths in honor of those who have lost their lives in military service. Watching from a balcony alongside Queen Camilla, the Princess wore a sharply tailored black Catherine Walker coat (a new addition to her wardrobe, from a long-favored designer that Diana also loved), with a double-breasted silhouette, velvet buttons, and a high velvet collar, topped with an asymmetric wide-brimmed hat by Jane Taylor. But it was the familiar pearl-and-diamond earrings that carried a particularly personal significance.
points: Over two days of remembrance, the Princess of Wales paid tribute to Queen Elizabeth II and Princess Diana through two particularly meaningful pieces of jewelry.

articles.title: This Golden-Hour Honolulu Wedding Shared the Same View as the Couple’s First Date
articles.summary: Set high above the Hawaiian capital, filmmaker Daniel Croix and producer Mele Hamasaki’s cinematic wedding featured ancestral rituals, handmade lei, and a sunset hula.
body: A tropical storm warning couldn’t stop Mele Hamasaki and Daniel Croix Henderson from going on their first date. “I think we both had a special feeling about each other and were just way too excited to postpone,” Mele says of their May 6, 2021 meeting. “The connection was instantaneous and life-altering.” Sitting at Tantalus Lookout in Honolulu, the two discussed nature, their creative processes, and more. “As we both had hoped, the storm never came,” says Mele. “Instead, we were blessed with a stunning sunset and an empty park entirely for us!”

“All these years later, I look at the life we’ve built together—our individual and shared dreams coming into focus, the films we’ve co-created, the communities we’ve rooted in, and the curiosity we still bring to one another—and realize our first date was a microcosm of everything that followed,” adds Daniel, an actor and filmmaker.

articles.title: The Wonder—and Weirdness—of Exploring a National Park in the Dark
articles.summary: Once the sun goes down and crowds disperse, nature comes alive. On a trip to Southern Utah, writer Jamie Spain finds a new way to see America’s parks after dark.
body: I’ve spent the majority of my life doing outdoor activities: camping, hiking, biking, kayaking, you name it. It’s intrinsically part of who I am, something that defines my siblings and I so deeply it feels like it’s braided into our DNA.

Perhaps that’s because, when I was just two-and-a-half years old, my parents took my siblings and me on a two-month-long road trip from New York to Arizona, hitting dozens of state and national parks on the way. We still talk about that adventure, lovingly referred to as the Out West Trip. It was the first time I visited Utah’s national parks, known as the Mighty 5: Zion, Arches, Canyonlands, Capitol Reef, and Bryce Canyon.
Once night falls in Utah's national parks, most travelers head back to their campfires or motor lodges—except for those willing to brave the dark and explore their nocturnal side.

body: Travel buffs can be surprisingly difficult to shop for. They probably already have a suitcase they love, noise-canceling headphones, and enough packing cubes to last them a lifetime. Instead of adding to their collection of travel essentials, consider something they wouldn't necessarily buy for themselves. It doesn't have to be expensive, either. The best travel gifts will upgrade every journey, whether it’s a smart gadget to help make a red-eye flight less miserable or a sweet reminder of their favorite destination—all without breaking the bank.

With this in mind, I’ve rounded up 50 thoughtful gifts under $50 to give this season, from personalized accessories to luxe skincare sets.
